1. `parseHttpRequest` returns `method`, `path`, and `query` as slices into its own local `header_buf`, so every caller receives dangling slices after the function returns and all later route checks and query parsing operate on invalid memory.[1]

2. `parseHttpRequest` stops reading headers when its fixed 8192-byte buffer fills, but it does not reject the request as too large and instead continues with truncated header data.[1]

3. `parseHttpRequest` accepts a body shorter than the declared `Content-Length` and passes that truncated body downstream instead of failing the request.[1]

4. `parseHttpRequest` silently treats bodies larger than 1 MiB as empty because it skips reading them but still returns a normal `HttpRequest`.[1]

5. `parseJsonField` is not a real JSON parser, so it can match a field name inside unrelated text or nested content and extract the wrong value.[1]

6. `parseJsonField` only skips spaces and `:` after the key, so valid JSON that uses tabs or newlines there can fail to parse.[1]

7. `parseJsonField` handles only a small subset of JSON escape sequences and misparses valid escapes such as `\uXXXX`, `\/`, `\b`, and `\f`.[1]

8. `parseJsonField` ignores allocation failures during string reconstruction with `catch {}`, so it can silently return truncated or corrupted values.[1]

9. `AgentRun.init` has no cleanup on partial failure, so if any later allocation fails after an earlier one succeeded, the already allocated fields and the struct itself leak.[1]

10. `AgentRun.setCurrentUrl` frees the old buffer before duplicating the new one, so an allocation failure leaves `current_url` pointing to freed memory.[1]

11. `AgentRun.setLastAction` has the same free-before-allocate bug, so an allocation failure leaves `last_action` as a dangling pointer.[1]

12. Finished or stopped runs are never removed from `run_registry` and never deinitialized, so every run leaks permanently.[1]

13. `main` never deinitializes `run_registry.map`, so the registry itself also leaks on shutdown.[1]

14. `handleStatus` reads `run.iteration`, `run.current_url`, and `run.last_action` while `agentLoop` mutates them without any shared synchronization, creating data races.[1]

15. `run.setCurrentUrl` and `run.setLastAction` replace heap-backed slices without any lock, so readers can observe torn state or freed memory concurrently.[1]

16. `handleStatus` formats `current_url` and `last_action` directly into JSON without escaping, so quotes, backslashes, or control characters make the response invalid JSON.[1]

17. `handleApiAgent` writes the initial `"Agent started"` SSE payload with the raw `message` embedded in JSON, so user input containing quotes or newlines breaks the event payload.[1]

18. `callLlmSimple` injects `user_message` directly into JSON without escaping, so many valid user inputs produce an invalid request body for the LLM API.[1]

19. `handleApiChat` builds the escaped SSE response with `catch {}` on every append, so allocation failures can silently truncate the emitted JSON.[1]

20. `agentLoop` builds `start_msg` with raw `current_url` and `page_title` inserted into JSON, so normal page titles containing quotes can break the SSE message.[1]

21. `agentLoop` builds `think_msg` with raw `llm_response` inserted into JSON, so any quoted or multiline model output can make the event invalid JSON.[1]

22. `agentLoop` builds `thought_msg` with raw `parsed_action.thought` inserted into JSON, which has the same invalid-JSON failure mode.[1]

23. `agentLoop` also inserts raw `target`, `value`, `extracted`, `action_result`, and action names into the navigation, click, type, scroll, extract, submit, and unknown-action SSE messages, so many normal values produce malformed JSON.[1]

24. The history entry appended in `agentLoop` is built as JSON from unescaped `action`, `target`, and `result`, so `history_entries` itself can become invalid JSON and then poison later prompts.[1]

25. `writeHttpResponse` maps every unknown status code to the reason phrase `"OK"`, so the 503 path in `handleScreenshot` sends `503 OK` instead of a matching reason phrase.[1]

26. `writeHttpResponse` swallows both header and body write failures with `catch {}`, so callers cannot tell when the response was not actually delivered.[1]

27. `writeSSEHeaders` also ignores write failures, so handlers can proceed into long SSE loops after the header send already failed.[1]

28. `callLlmWithMessages` never checks the HTTP status line before parsing the body, so API errors and normal success responses are handled through the same fragile parsing path.[1]

29. `callLlmWithMessages` detects chunked transfer encoding with a case-sensitive substring search for `"chunked"`, so differently cased but valid headers are missed.[1]

30. `decodeChunked` does not support chunk extensions and does not verify the required trailing `\r\n` after each chunk, so valid or malformed chunked responses can be decoded incorrectly.[1]

31. `callLlmForAgent` allocates `escaped_task`, `escaped_url`, `escaped_title`, `escaped_dom`, and `escaped_history` and then never uses them, which is dead work on every iteration.[1]

32. `CdpClient.call` waits only for a matching numeric `id` and ignores whether the matching response contains a CDP `"error"` object, so protocol failures are treated like success.[1]

33. `CdpClient.evaluate` throws away valid JavaScript results of type boolean, null, object, and array by returning an empty string for all of them.[1]

34. `clickElement` interpolates the raw CSS selector directly into a JavaScript string literal without escaping, so selectors containing quotes or backslashes break the script.[1]

35. `extractText` calls `el.textContent.trim()` without guarding against `textContent == null`, so it can throw even when the element exists.[1]

36. `submitForm` always returns `"ok"` even when the selector matches nothing or a non-form element, so it reports success for failed submissions.[1]

37. `getDomSnapshot` generates fallback selectors with `:nth-child(i+1)` where `i` is the index in the filtered result set, not the element’s actual sibling index under its parent, so those selectors are often wrong.[1]

38. `getDomSnapshot` builds selectors from raw `id` and `name` values without CSS escaping, so perfectly valid DOM values can produce invalid selectors.[1]

39. `startChrome` hardcodes a single Nix-store Chromium path, so the program fails outside that exact machine layout.[1]

40. The code hardcodes port `9222` in multiple places such as the Chrome launch args and `/json` Host header instead of consistently using `CHROME_DEBUG_PORT`, so changing the constant does not actually retarget the whole program.[1]

41. `startChrome` hardcodes `--user-data-dir=/tmp/agent-chrome-profile`, so concurrent instances collide and old browser state bleeds into later runs.[1]

42. `main` spawns a detached OS thread for every accepted connection with no limit or pooling, which scales poorly and can exhaust resources under load.[1]

43. `handleEvents` and `handleApiAgent` busy-poll every 200 ms even though `SseQueue` has a condition variable, and that condition variable is never actually waited on anywhere.[1]

44. The `history` variable created in `agentLoop` is initialized and written once but never read, so it is dead code.[1]

45. `const AgentLoopArgs = struct { run: *AgentRun }` is declared but never used anywhere.[1]

46. `CdpClient.sendFrame` and `CdpClient.recvFrame` handle 64-bit WebSocket lengths incorrectly by encoding and decoding only the low 32 bits when the 127-length form is used.[1]

47. `CdpClient.recvFrame` returns `fin` for ping frames and `recvMessage` treats that as end-of-message, so a ping can produce a bogus empty message and interfere with fragmented-message assembly.[1]

48. `getChromeTargetUrl` reads Chrome’s `/json` endpoint as a plain HTTP body and never decodes chunked transfer encoding there, so a chunked response would be parsed incorrectly.[1]

49. `handleStop` only flips `run.running` and does not interrupt ongoing CDP or LLM calls, so a run can keep executing for a long time after the stop endpoint reports success.[1]

50. that’s all.

1. `agentLoop` creates `step_arena` inside the loop and uses `defer step_arena.deinit();`, so all per-iteration allocations are retained until the whole function exits instead of being released at the end of each iteration.[1]

2. `agentLoop` stores `history_entries` in the outer arena allocator, so every accumulated history string lives until the run ends with no trimming or cap, causing unbounded memory growth across iterations.[1]

3. `agentLoop` assigns `run.iteration = iter + 1` from the worker thread while other threads read it without atomic access or locking, creating a race.[1]

4. `agentLoop` reads `run.current_url` in the fallback path for `cdp.getCurrentUrl()` while other threads may read or overwrite that same field concurrently, which is another unsynchronized shared-memory access.[1]

5. `agentLoop` falls back to `step_alloc.dupe(u8, run.current_url)` after `cdp.getCurrentUrl()` fails, but because `run.current_url` itself is concurrently mutable and may be dangling due to `setCurrentUrl`, that fallback can duplicate invalid memory.[1]

6. `agentLoop` uses case-sensitive substring checks for Cloudflare challenge detection, so title variants with different casing are missed.[1]

7. `agentLoop` detects challenge pages only from title substrings and `"challenge"` in the URL, so many bot-block pages outside those exact phrases are misclassified and the control logic becomes unreliable.[1]

8. `agentLoop` sleeps for 5 seconds on a detected challenge but does not record that as a history action, so the LLM prompt omits a meaningful prior action and weakens state continuity.[1]

9. `const history_str = history_entries.items; const hist_json = fmt.allocPrint(step_alloc, "{s}", .{history_str})` is pointless copying of the already assembled history slice.[1]

10. `agentLoop` allocates `hist_json` but never frees it until the function exits because it comes from the per-iteration arena that is incorrectly deferred to the function end.[1]

11. `agentLoop` pushes a parse-error event and simply continues when the LLM returns malformed JSON, but it does not add that failure to structured history, so the model gets no feedback about repeated invalid outputs.[1]

12. `agentLoop` sets `run.last_action` to `parsed_action.action` before the action is actually executed, so `/status` can report an action that never successfully happened.[1]

13. `agentLoop` initializes `action_result` to `"ok"` before branching, which means paths like `wait` and `done` implicitly inherit a success result string without a real action result being computed.[1]

14. The `navigate` branch logs success text regardless of what `Page.navigate` actually returned because `cdp.navigate` discards the protocol response content and only sleeps.[1]

15. The `click` branch reports success whenever `clickElement`’s JS evaluates without transport failure, even though `clickElement` itself ignores the returned `"not found"` vs `"ok"` value.[1]

16. The `type` branch has the same false-success problem because `typeText` ignores whether the DOM script returned `"not found"` or `"ok"`.[1]

17. The `scroll` branch treats any unrecognized direction as downward scrolling because `scrollPage` does `if direction == "up" then -amt else amt`.[1]

18. The `extract` branch never copies the extracted text into persistent task state beyond a log message, so later iterations do not actually retain the extracted result except as free-form history text.[1]

19. The `submit` branch reports success whenever the JS runs, even though `submitForm` returns `"ok"` even for missing elements.[1]

20. The `wait` branch hardcodes 4 seconds, but the system prompt tells the model only to use `"wait"` with empty target and value; there is no adaptive waiting based on page state or navigation completion.[1]

21. `agentLoop` handles unknown actions only by logging them and continuing, without normalizing them, rejecting them, or steering the run toward termination, so a bad model can waste all iterations.[1]

22. `agentLoop` appends history entries as a comma-separated pseudo-array but manually prepends commas with `if history_entries.items.len > 0 history_entries.appendSlice(",")`, which is fragile string-building instead of using a JSON writer.[1]

23. The history entry string in `agentLoop` uses unescaped interpolated fields, so quotes or backslashes in any action data can corrupt the history JSON-like structure sent to the model.[1]

24. `if (iter + 1 == run.max_iterations) { const limit_msg = "{\"type\":\"content\",\"text\":\"Max iterations reached\"}"; run.sse_queue.push(limit_msg); }` reports the limit only on the exact last loop body, but if the run exits earlier due to `run.running` becoming false the user gets no explicit stop reason.[1]

25. `parseAgentAction` tries to strip markdown fences by checking only whether the trimmed response starts with ``` and ends with ```, which misses many common fenced-output variants and malformed fence placements.[1]

26. `parseAgentAction` searches for the first `{` and then tracks brace depth without any awareness of JSON strings, so a `{` or `}` inside a quoted string breaks object extraction.[1]

27. `parseAgentAction` never verifies that it actually found a matching closing brace after depth tracking; if none is found, `end_pos` remains at `start` and `clean_json` becomes an invalid slice.[1]

28. `parseAgentAction` defaults the action to `"navigate"` when the `action` field is missing or not a string, which can cause arbitrary navigation from malformed model output instead of safely failing.[1]

29. `parseAgentAction` defaults `done` to `action == "done"` even if the response explicitly contained an invalid non-boolean `done` field, silently accepting malformed schema.[1]

30. `parseAgentAction` allocates duplicate strings for every parsed field even though the parsed JSON object already lives for the duration of the function, causing unnecessary allocation churn.[1]

31. `main` uses `defer gpa.deinit();` without checking its returned leak status, so allocator-detected leaks are ignored.[1]

32. `main` continues starting the HTTP server even when `startChrome()` fails, but several endpoints such as `/screenshot` and all agent features depend on Chrome, so the process advertises functionality that is partially broken from startup.[1]

33. `main` binds to `0.0.0.0:8080` unconditionally, exposing the service on all interfaces with no configuration switch.[1]

34. `main` accepts connections forever with no shutdown handling, signal handling, or coordinated cleanup of active runs and detached threads.[1]

35. On `Thread.spawn` failure in the accept loop, `main` closes only `conn.stream` and not the whole `net.Server.Connection` abstraction explicitly, relying on internals rather than symmetric cleanup.[1]

36. `handleConn` routes `/events`, `/status`, `/stop`, and `/screenshot` without checking HTTP method, so unsupported methods are incorrectly accepted for those endpoints.[1]

37. `handleConn` has no branch for `OPTIONS`, but it emits `Access-Control-Allow-Origin: *`, so browser CORS preflight for JSON POST requests can still fail.[1]

38. `writeHttpResponse` omits a `charset` for text responses like `"Bad Request"` and `"Not Found"`, while other responses do include UTF-8 text, leading to inconsistent text response metadata.[1]

39. `handleTaskPost` uses `const run_id = &id_buf;` and later formats that into JSON, which works only because `AgentRun.init` duplicates it immediately; the local-slice style is fragile and easy to misuse elsewhere.[1]

40. `handleTaskPost` returns the locally generated `run_id` string rather than `run.id`, so if initialization or duplication logic ever changes, the response could diverge from the stored identifier.[1]

41. `handleEvents` obtains `run` from the registry and then uses it indefinitely, but the registry does not provide lifetime management, so if future code ever frees runs on completion this handler would become use-after-free prone.[1]

42. `handleEvents` never sends heartbeat comments or ping events, so many proxies or clients may close long-lived idle SSE connections prematurely.[1]

43. `handleEvents` polls `run.sse_queue.isDone()` separately from `drain()`, so messages pushed between the drain and done check can be reordered relative to the terminal `"done"` event.[1]

44. `handleApiAgent` duplicates nearly the same SSE draining loop as `handleEvents`, creating duplicated control flow and duplicated future bug surface.[1]

45. `handleApiAgent` creates a run and immediately streams it on the same connection, but it also stores the same run in the global registry, meaning the same run may be observed through two independently polling SSE consumers with no coordination.[1]

46. `handleApiAgent` sends an `agent_run_id` event before validating that later SSE writes continue to succeed, so clients can receive a started run id even when the stream effectively dies immediately after.[1]

47. `handleApiChat` gets the API key with the request-scoped arena allocator and then uses it in a network call that may outlive some intermediate buffers, making allocator lifetime coupling harder to reason about than necessary.[1]

48. `escapeJsonString` uses `fmt.bufPrint(&tmp, "\\u{x:0>4}", .{c})` for control characters, which is correct only for byte values, but the function otherwise treats the input as UTF-8 bytes and does not validate UTF-8, so malformed UTF-8 passes through unchecked into JSON strings.[1]

49. `extractLlmContent` assumes `message.content` is a plain string, but chat APIs may return structured or multimodal content arrays, so valid responses can be rejected.[1]

50. `CdpClient.connect` verifies only that the response starts with `HTTP/1.1 101` and does not validate `Upgrade`, `Connection`, or `Sec-WebSocket-Accept`, so it accepts incomplete or bogus upgrade responses.[1]
